opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, because I think people often imagine it as this binary thing — either you're "vibe coding" and letting the model write everything, or you're a purist who writes every line by hand. For me it's really somewhere in the middle, and it depends a lot on the task.

When I'm working on something where correctness and understanding really matter — like when I'm implementing an architecture from scratch for a book chapter, say a new attention variant or a normalization layer — I mostly write the code myself. The whole point there is that I want to understand every detail, and if I let the LLM generate it, I'd end up reading it anyway and maybe missing subtle bugs. Writing it is kind of how I think through it. I might still use the model as a sounding board, like, "Does this match what the paper describes?" or "Why might these shapes not line up?" But the core logic is mine.

On the other end, there's a lot of what I'd call boilerplate or glue work — writing a plotting function, setting up argument parsing, converting some data format, writing a quick unit test scaffold. That's where I'm very happy to let the LLM do most of the work. It's tedious, it's well-trodden, and it's easy to verify by just looking at the output. That saves me a lot of time.

And then there's this middle zone where I use it more like a smart autocomplete or a pair programmer. I'll write a function signature and a docstring and see what it suggests, then edit it. Or I'll paste in an error message and some context when I'm debugging. I find that very productive because I stay in control, but I'm not typing everything.

The one thing I try to be careful about is not outsourcing the understanding. It's very tempting, especially when the code runs, to just move on. But in research code especially, code that runs isn't the same as code that's correct. A silent bug in how you compute a loss or mask tokens can mess up your results without crashing anything. So the rule I follow is: if I couldn't explain what a piece of code does, it doesn't go into anything I care about.

So, short answer: I'm a heavy user, but more on the "assisted" side than the "autonomous agent" side — at least for the work that matters most to me.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes “vibe coding” as letting the model write everything, but does not say the term understates LLM use when an entire product is built without manual coding.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say I'm somewhere in the middle, honestly, and it depends a lot on what I'm doing.

When I'm writing code that I actually want to understand, like the implementations for my books or the from-scratch notebooks, I use LLMs very sparingly. The whole point of that work is that I know what every line does, so if I let a model generate a chunk of the attention mechanism, I've kind of defeated the purpose. There I might use it like a smarter autocomplete, or to ask "is there a cleaner way to express this tensor reshape," but I'm still the one driving.

On the other end, for throwaway stuff, I'm much more relaxed. Plotting scripts, converting a dataset format, writing a little script to scrape results out of log files, that kind of thing. I don't really care about elegance there, I just want it to work, and I'll happily let a model write most of it and just skim it.

What I don't do, at least not yet, is the fully hands-off, "build me this feature and I'll look at it tomorrow" style. Partly that's because the projects I work on are small enough that I can keep them in my head, and partly it's a trust thing. I've seen models produce code that looks completely plausible and is subtly wrong, especially around things like numerical details, and in research code those bugs can be very expensive because they don't crash, they just quietly give you a slightly different result.

So I think the way I'd frame it is: the less I'm going to read the code, the more I'm willing to delegate. And the more I'm trying to learn something or make a claim based on it, the more I want to write it myself.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they do not use a fully hands-off approach and never suggests that “vibe coding” understates building an entire product without manual coding.

astra-6.text:
I’d say I’m somewhere in the middle. I still like to write code myself, especially when I’m working on something where understanding the details is really the point. If I’m implementing a model or trying out a research idea, I don’t want to outsource that thinking, because writing the code is part of how I figure out whether I actually understand it.

But I’m happy to use an LLM to help with repetitive work, to suggest a starting point, or to help me debug something. Sometimes it’s just useful to have another way of looking at a problem. The distinction for me is whether I can evaluate what it gives me. If I understand the code and can test it, it can save a lot of time. If it produces something I don’t understand, then I still have work to do before I’m comfortable using it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes using LLMs for repetitive work, starting points, and debugging while still writing code for research or model implementation. It does not suggest that “vibe coding” understates building an entire product without manual coding.

sol-6.1.text:
I would say I’m somewhere in the middle. I use LLMs quite a bit, but usually for relatively small, well-defined tasks. If I’m writing research code, the implementation is often part of how I develop my understanding, so I want to stay very involved in that process. Having a model write the whole thing would take away some of the work I actually want to do.

But there are plenty of things around that core work where it’s useful: writing a little utility, helping with plotting code, or suggesting a way to simplify something. In those cases, I can describe what I need, look at the result, and check it fairly quickly.

So, for me, it depends on what I’m trying to get out of the task. If the goal is to learn or explore an idea, I tend to do more of it myself. If I know what I want and just need to get it implemented, I’m much more happy to delegate parts of that to an LLM.

r001.rationale: The response describes using LLMs for small, well-defined tasks and delegating parts of implementation. It does not say that “vibe coding” understates LLM use when an entire product is built without manual coding.
